body: Mykola expects to drive his battered beige passenger minibus 20 to 24 times a day past the holes in the road on Kyiv’s damaged Northern Bridge that were caused by a Russian ballistic missile attack on Tuesday.

Buses are now the only motor transport allowed across the normally busy multi-lane crossing, though on their way into the city centre they have to skirt the tears in the tarmac, using the only functioning lane to get by.
“So what if there’s a hole? The bridge hasn’t collapsed. You need to know a bit about bridge construction,” says Mykola, 65, at the wheel of a half -full afternoon bus as it clatters on its way west.

Mykola operates a marshrutka, a single deck private bus, whose drivers are famed in Kyiv mythology for being able to multi-task: chatting, smoking and collecting fares, while driving as fast as possible to take passengers from rivals.

Passengers pay 25 hryvnia (42p) in cash and typically one passenger gets the unofficial job of taking money and handing back change on behalf of the driver. It turns out this has become the Guardian’s task, in order to conduct an interview.

“It would be very difficult to destroy the bridge. It would take a huge number of missiles, and if one or two hit it, it wouldn’t be the end of the world,” Mykola continues, with behind-the-wheel speculation that is so far accurate. By lunchtime the holes have been covered up, perhaps to avoid unsettling passengers eyeing the Dnipro River below.

Alongside its attacks on the capital’s electricity, heating and water systems, Russia has been attacking Kyiv’s bridges since early October, trying to cut off the city centre in the west from the newer, largely residential east, home to about a third of its population.

Moscow struck the bridges twice again this week, first on Tuesday – overshadowed by Ukraine’s partial destruction of the Kerch road bridge to Crimea. Then again during a noisy Thursday night, hours after Vladimir Putin promised there would be a “far more painful” response to the demolition of his pet project.

As of Friday, in an already traffic-snarled city, Kyiv’s other main road bridge, the Southern Bridge, was allowing motor traffic only from east to west. The new Podilskyi Bridge, damaged early on Friday, was similarly restricted, and the city’s mayor, Vitali Klitschko, told people to avoid car travel after a night in which six were killed.

The Northern Bridge remains open for public transport – plus any cyclists, scooter riders and walkers willing to brave the damp late autumn weather and ignore missile and drone alerts. But below, earthworks have begun to prepare for a floating pontoon bridge, one of eight planned, in case of the worst.

Dmytro Bespalov, a transport planning expert with Kyiv’s National University of Construction and Architecture, said it was difficult to destroy a suspension bridge like the Northern. They have “a strong construction, with a lot of repairability”, meaning damage can usually be fixed. Though there are holes in the roadway, its supporting structures were so far unscathed, he added.

Russia is thought to have been aiming ballistic missiles at the supporting pylon, requiring a precise and difficult to execute attack, though that is what Ukraine did at the culmination of its complex attack on the Kerch road bridge, which was brought down after a Flamingo cruise missile struck its supporting arch.

Yet, Bespalov cautioned that Kyiv was strategically vulnerable if Russia targets the bridges with “dozens or hundreds” of missiles, because the city did not have enough bridges from before the war. “In 2021, Kyiv was in third place in Europe for congestion on the TomTom traffic index,” he said, behind Istanbul and Moscow.

Particular concern is reserved for the pontoon bridge alternative. They can bear less traffic: “It would take 20 pontoon bridges to have half the current capacity,” Bespalov said – and they are far more vulnerable to missile and drone attack. “I don’t think it would be possible to use pontoons during a red [missile] or yellow [drone] alarm” – not least because vehicles could end up in the water.

At the first busy bus stop on the eastern left bank, Nataliya, 40, and Iryna, 39, are happy to make the crossing over the Northern Bridge. They say they have long got used to the difficulties of war: “The main thing is to get through the first 24 hours at home after the initial discomfort, and then we’ll adapt,” said Nataliya, a customer service specialist.

Iryna added: “If we start to despair, that’s exactly what they want. A bridge can be built. The main thing is that when the attack comes, there are no civilians or military personnel around. It’s just concrete, that’s all. They’ll either repair it or come up with something new.”

It is a core attitude of Kyiv’s remaining residents, who are already contending with hours of electricity shortages and a lack of heating, with the full chill of winter yet to arrive. People want to deal with problems as they arise rather than worrying excessively about what may come – though it is not always easy amid the daily attacks, including a daytime raid on Thursday in which a drone exploded near the Dutch embassy.

Oleksandr, 42, a construction worker, was waiting to get across the bridge. “If the bridges are destroyed we’ll have to leave,” he conceded. If that happened, he and his wife would move to her parents’ house across the river. “I bought them a generator there; they have their own water well. We’d already dug the well during the war. They used to have gas heating, but we’ve converted it to wood-burning. We’re preparing,” he said.
Additional reporting by Galya Rudyk

articles.title: Tourists are throwing fewer coins into Rome’s Trevi fountain – is €2 entry fee to blame?
articles.summary: Charity that collects the coins says donations are down by £200,000 after a barrier was put in place to restrict access
body: When Jeff Clinton, an American visiting Rome with his wife for the first time, found a US one-cent coin on a street close to Termini train station, he knew precisely what he was going to do with it. “I’ll throw it into the Trevi fountain,” said Clinton, holding the copper coin in the palm of his hand as the couple admired the landmark.

He was well aware of the tradition among tourists of tossing a coin over their shoulder and into the waters of the baroque masterpiece, in a ritual fabled to ensure a return visit to the city or make other dreams come true.

But the only thing holding him back from partaking in the gesture was the distance: the steps towards the fountain’s sunken basin are separated by a low barrier and accessible during the day only by Rome’s residents or visitors who pay €2 (£1.64).

The fee, in place since February, has been partly blamed for taking some of the allure out of the coin-throwing tradition. The Rome unit of the church-run charity Caritas, which sweeps up the Trevi fountain’s coins, usually brings in more than €1.4m a year. But it noted a shortfall of about €200,000 between January and September compared with the same period in 2025.

“The closure of the direct access to the Trevi fountain might be a factor,” Giustino Trincia, the director of Caritas Roma, told Il Messaggero. The charity uses the donations to fund food banks and other welfare projects.
Clinton did contemplate asking someone in the basin area to throw the coin into the fountain on his behalf, but in the end slipped it back into his pocket.
The shift towards contactless payments and mobile phone wallets is also believed to have eroded Caritas’s collections.

Eric and Patty, a young couple from New York, said they might have thrown a coin, but did not have any change. Neither did they want to pay the €2 fee to get close to the basin. “It’s such a breathtaking monument, we’re happy just to take it in from here,” said Patty as they posed for selfies.
Alan and Ying, visiting Rome from Australia, did pay the fee. While they had heard that throwing coins “is what people do”, they decided not to indulge because “nobody else was really doing it”.
“I always carry cash with me because you never know when you might need it,” said Ying. “But we didn’t see anyone else doing it, so we didn’t either.”

A spokesperson for Caritas Rome told the Guardian the charity was not making any further public statements about the dwindling coin collection. The spokesperson said the collection so far this year did not take into account foreign currency coins, so the hit might not be so bad.
Still, the matter is understood to have caused friction with Rome’s council, which generated €435,194 from the access fee within the first month of its inception.

The initiative is aimed at curbing overcrowding at the monument while raising funds for the upkeep of the fountain and other Rome monuments. No further figures have been published, but with 4.4 million tourists flocking to the Trevi in 2025, the fee had been forecast to generate a tidy income for the council each year.

A team of stewards staff the ticketing system and monitor the flow of the crowd in the basin area. Nicolas Romero does shifts of seven or eight hours. He said people quite often asked him for change in order to throw a coin. “But many don’t even seem to know about the tradition,” he said. “This might also explain the decline.”

The gesture is believed to have its origins in an ancient pagan ritual offering to the water gods, although the custom of throwing coins only really took off globally after the 1954 romantic comedy film, Three Coins in the Fountain.

articles.title: ‘We ​are tired from all this suffering’: displaced families in Gaza brace for another winter of misery
articles.summary: Floods have worsened harsh existence for Palestinians living in tent camps, with fears growing for what the coming months will bring
body: Abdul Karim al-Sahhar knew winter was coming to Gaza in the small hours of a wet and windy night earlier this month when a sandbank collapsed just yards from his makeshift tent, killing four people.
“It was a terrifying scene. I could not process what I was seeing,” the 30-year-old said. “My legs felt frozen from the shock. I found my mother buried under the sand.

“We got [my mother] out but we saw [other] people buried beneath the sand and rocks. None of them was moving or making a sound. The next door tent had disappeared completely. There was no trace of it left.”

Al-Sahhar is originally from Beit Hanoun in northern Gaza, which was almost entirely destroyed in the early weeks of the two-year war in the territory. Its ruins now lie on the side of the “yellow line” dividing Gaza that is controlled by Israel.

The collapse of the sandbank in the southern coastal zone of al-Mawasi was triggered by heavy rain. As the weather gets worse in the coming weeks and months, experts say there will be more such tragedies.
“This happens every winter, every winter is very harsh, you have an ongoing natural disaster,” said Wadhah Hubaishi, a regional director of the World Central Kitchen.
Aid officials in Gaza said the poorest, disabled people, elderly and sick people would suffer most, though few will escape the coming months unscathed.

Al-Sahhar, a former municipal rubbish worker, has no job, no income and no savings. He was badly injured during the war, which left Gaza in ruins, with more than 80% of buildings damaged and basic infrastructure such as roads and sanitation systems shattered.

“My family and I are living in great fear,” said al-Sahhar. “But honestly, I cannot find anywhere else to go. There are no available places for us, and even the places that can be rented have become extremely expensive. Where am I supposed to get the money to pay the rent?”

Al-Mawasi is now crowded with tents housing some of the near 2 million people displaced in Gaza. There is very limited sanitation, water or other essentials. The recent rains affected more than 220,000 people and damaged more than 40,000 shelters, the UN said.

The US-backed Board of Peace, a body set up to implement the October 2025 ceasefire deal, last week accused Israel and Hamas of failing to honour their commitments to end hostilities, warning that “a ceasefire that delivers nothing visible cannot be sustained indefinitely”.

While the ceasefire halted major ⁠fighting, the wider plan, which calls for Hamas to disarm, Israeli troops to withdraw and reconstruction to begin, has stalled. Gaza’s health ministry has said that more than 1,600 Palestinians have been killed by Israel since the 2025 ceasefire.

Hamas agreed in July to a roadmap to surrender its weapons and transfer governance of Gaza to a civilian transitional authority, but Israel said it would not withdraw its forces until Hamas has disarmed.

Israeli military forces control about 70% of Gaza, and this week Israel launched its highest-profile ground incursion across the yellow line since major fighting ended more than a year ago, forcing dozens of displaced Palestinians to flee their tents. The raid targeted a suspected Hamas tunnel, Israeli officials said.

Under the ceasefire deal, Israel agreed to allow 18,000 trucks into Gaza each month. But data obtained by the Israeli newspaper Haaretz shows the number has never exceeded 13,000 since March. In some months, fewer than 5,000 trucks entered Gaza. NGOs also say that vehicles entering Gaza with humanitarian aid are often carrying only a partial load.

“Israeli policies continue to obstruct the entry of critical items as well as access to most of Gaza’s land, including areas away from the shoreline that are less prone to flooding,” the UN said in a statement. “Incoming supplies face multiple approval requirements, limited crossing capacity and unpredictable or narrow delivery windows that delay their entry.”
Mubashisaid his organisation had broken up wooden food pallets to make wooden tent poles, used old food sacks for sandbags and supplied worn out metal pots to build flood defences.
Aid officials said that with spare parts repeatedly being blocked by Israeli authorities, efforts to maintain critical equipment after years of heavy use were reaching their limit.
Last week, Australia, Canada, the UK and Italy urged Israel to allow 150,000 tents and other vital supplies being held at the border into Gaza before winter.

Israeli officials say that more than 93,000 tents and more than 8,600 trucks carrying winter supplies and other essential equipment, such as laboratory supplies, engine oil and incubator parts, have entered Gaza.

Most of the supplies entering the territory are brought in by a very small number of commercial operators and sold on the open market. Fresh meat and vegetables, as well as a wide range of non-essential food products such as chocolate and snacks, are available but unaffordable for the vast majority of Palestinians in Gaza.
The UN estimates that up to two-thirds of the population in Gaza are experiencing severe food shortages through the end of 2026, only a slight reduction from the 77% at the end of 2025.

Mohammad Shafoot, the owner of Shafoot Restaurant, one of Gaza’s oldest, said he had done brisk business in the immediate aftermath of the ceasefire but that patrons were now limited to employees of international and local organisations, traders and their families.
“The problem today is not simply whether goods are available, but that many people do not have enough money to buy what they need or eat at restaurants,” Shafoot said.
Emad al-Ghoul, the secretary general of the North Gaza Chamber of Commerce, said there had been no real improvement in the commercial or economic situation since the ceasefire.

“The industrial sector has almost completely come to a standstill, with an estimated 95% of local industry no longer operating,” al-Ghoul said. “Trade in general has become concentrated in the hands of a small number of merchants. This has led to a lack of competition in the market and rising prices, with ordinary citizens ultimately bearing the consequences.”
Only 3% of Gaza’s farming land remains accessible and undamaged, according to an August geospatial assessment by the UN. The rest is in the Israeli-occupied zone.
Israeli airstrikes have intensified in recent weeks, and there are frequent clashes between Hamas forces and Israeli-backed militia operating from bases over the yellow line.

“We ​are tired from all this suffering. We need someone to find a solution ‌for us ... Those who live in tents, ‌they drown. Those who are on the streets, they get wounded. Those who are here, they get wounded,” Abd Aliwa, 44, said as he sat beside a pile of rubble in the Nuseirat refugee camp, the target of Israel’s incursion last week.

The death toll in Gaza since October 2023, when Hamas launched a surprise attack into Israel and killed 1,200, mostly civilians, has now reached 74,000, mostly civilians. In June, an ⁠independent UN inquiry determined that Israel was continuing to commit genocide by deliberately targeting Palestinian children.

Mohammad Abu Daqqa, originally from the city of Khan Younis, now lives with his wife and seven children in a tattered tent in al-Qarara on the coast. The 39-year-old former agricultural worker has earned nothing since the beginning of the war. His father, brother and two nephews were killed in the war, and his daughter injured by shrapnel in her leg.

“Winter has become a recurring struggle for us,” Abu Daqqa said. “This is the third winter I have spent with my family in the same place … and each year we face the same conditions: cold, rain and strong winds. The tent is now worn out and cannot withstand the weather. My children have to hold on to the edges of the tent to stop it from blowing away or tearing apart.”

The family have dug a shallow trench to protect their home, but know it offers very limited protection against surging seawater. Communal kitchens provide some food, and hot meals come from World Central Kitchen. Abu Baqqa can afford no washing powder or soap, which his wife is forced to beg from other displaced families.
“All I wish for is an end to this suffering and the chance to live in a proper shelter that preserves my dignity and protects my family,” he said.

articles.title: When you see smoke, run: Rohingya who escaped Myanmar’s genocide tell their stories
articles.summary: Survivors recount rivers red with blood and burning nearby villages serving as an urgent warning to flee their homes
body: Smoke was often the signal to run – seen from a distance, it was the indication for Rohingya that a neighbouring village was under attack and that theirs would be next.
In other places, they saw the rivers run red and would pull out the bodies, perform quick burial rites and then flee.

What happened during the escape from Myanmar – a journey through forests and over hills and rivers while being battered by monsoon rains – was a key part of the ruling made this week in The Hague that Myanmar had carried out a genocide against the Rohingya.

The international court of justice (ICJ) said it was not enough to say they had faced ethnic cleansing when soldiers had also killed those trying to escape – Myanmar was trying to destroy the group as a people.

Stories of that violence in 2017, of organised mass killing, sexual attacks and the complete destruction of their villages, came with the refugees who arrived in neighbouring Bangladesh, eventually numbering more than 700,000 and settling in what has become the world’s largest refugee camp.
Related: US reacts cautiously to Myanmar genocide ruling as EU praises ‘critical’ role of UN’s top court
For months, they would arrive from places such as Tula Toli, where thousands were rounded up, killed and buried in mass graves. In other villages, men were captured and killed by the security forces.
Many survivors had escaped an attack on their own village, only to watch their relatives being killed in the villages where they had sought safety.

Almost a decade later, the majority of Rohingya who arrived in 2017 remain in the refugee camps, joining those who had already been there since the early 1990s, having escaped previous military operations and ever-increasing persecution.

The ICJ ruling has come at a particularly harsh time for Rohingya refugees, in a year in which hundreds have died at sea trying to escape the refugee camps, and in which countries such as Malaysia and India have spoken about returning the Rohingya to Myanmar.
Rohingya campaigners are hoping that this ruling will put an end to that.
Rohingya refugees still live in fragile shelters made of bamboo and tarpaulin sheets. They are denied the right to leave the camps, to work or to seek education.
Below are some of the stories from Rohingya who arrived in Bangladesh in 2017, having escaped Tula Toli and the surrounding area.

Sitting in the background, almost unnoticed as Momtaz Begum recollected how Myanmar forces had killed her husband and children and then raped her in front of her lone surviving child, was a woman who seemed to know every word of the story.
It was not because she had heard it before. Dildar Begum had experienced exactly the same violence as her sister had, in their village, Tula Toli.
In fact, they had for months believed each other dead until they discovered that they had both made it to Bangladesh and lived in different parts of the camp.
Each had only one surviving daughter, both of whom had similar scars along the back of their heads.

Twice previously Anwara Begum had lived as a refugee in Bangladesh. Once as a child in 1978 and then again in the early 1990s, as a young mother who lost her son to a respiratory disease during a rainy season spent in a flimsy tent.
Related: Myanmar ruling gives new relevance to genocide convention and is ‘full of messages’ for Israel
When she was forced to return to Myanmar, though the persecution she fled there had not stopped, Anwara swore to herself that she would never become a refugee again.
She broke that oath when she saw the river by her village filled with bodies floating from Tula Toli.
Her husband first pulled from the river as many bodies as he could to bury and then they gathered some belongings and headed westwards to the River Naf – the border with Bangladesh.
To cross, she handed over all the gold she owned, equal to US $200 (£150), to a Bangladeshi boatman.
Elderly people were not spared the Myanmar military’s attacks. Like so many others, Nur Alam had to be carried on the shoulders of his children on his journey to Bangladesh.
His 10-year-old grandson, Mamoon, held his hand. Once in the camp, they stuck to each other.

Alam’s arrival in Bangladesh was his fourth time being a refugee there. He was first expelled from Myanmar – known as Burma until 1989 – during military operations in the 1950s when Bangladesh was not yet an independent country.

articles.title: French police officers found guilty of racist assault on black music producer
articles.summary: Beating of Michel Zecler in 2020 sparked outrage over police brutality after it was caught on security cameras
body: Three French police officers who beat a black music producer they said was not wearing a face mask during the Covid pandemic have been found guilty of intentional, racist violence.

The brutal assault on Michel Zecler, now 47, was caught on security cameras in his building in 2020 and triggered outrage in France over police brutality. The trial this month was considered a turning point for the recognition of racist violence.
The officers were sentenced to between one and two years in prison, with additional years suspended. They were banned for life from serving in the police.

The officers had stopped Zecler outside his Paris music studio on 21 November 2020, accusing him of failing to wear a mandatory face mask. They pushed him into the entrance of his office and violently beat him in an assault recorded by his studio’s security cameras.

Zecler sustained about 30 punches and truncheon blows to the face and body over a five-minute period, according to the investigation. He was left with craniofacial trauma, a wound to the lip and scalp, and a complete rupture of his biceps tendon, leaving him unable to work for 45 days.

Zecler told the court the officers used a racist slur against him on several occasions during the beating. He said the attack had “completely devastated him” and had left a lasting physical and psychological impact.

The three officers, Aurelien Lapersonne, 29, Pierre Plantier, 37, and Philippe Tondeux, 50, were found guilty of breaking into Zecler’s studio and committing intentional violence in a group. The judges decided racism was an aggravating factor in the attack.

The officers were also found guilty of forgery after they tried to cover up their actions by falsifying an official police report saying Zecler had been violent towards them. The police used that report to accuse Zecler of attacking them and trying to grab one of their weapons, but the video footage did not back up the claims, showing he was not violent.

The state prosecutor said that without the CCTV footage, the false police report on Zecler could have resulted in him being convicted of attacking a police officer in what would have been a serious miscarriage of justice.
The state prosecutor, who asked not to be named in the media, told the court the case had caused “immense harm to Michel Zecler but also to society as a whole”.
She said the officers had “betrayed” their uniform. She told the judges: “I ask you to believe Michel Zecler, to recognise him as a victim of these racist insults.”
The three police officers, who had not realised their attack was being recorded on security cameras, had apologised in court for beating Zecler, but denied racism.

Zecler’s lawyers and supporters said the trial had shone a spotlight on police violence in France, which victims and researchers say is systemic but authorities and law enforcement unions say is limited to isolated cases. Many members of the public who had come to support Zecler and watch the trial said it was an important moment in confronting institutionalised racism.

One of Zecler’s lawyers, Serge Money, said while summing up the case: “A verdict can force a society to really look at an injustice that up until now had been tolerated, minimised, and I dare to use the word: institutionalised.”
He said: “The Zecler trial is the trial of impunity, for all those who before him and after him will experience the same thing.”
Money told the court: “I want you to give voice to all those who didn’t have security cameras, and to all those who were not believed.”
Nine young performers who had been rehearsing in the basement at Zecler’s studio had been violently arrested when they came to assist Zecler.
Their lawyer, Seydi Ba, told the court that France needed to know how “police violence, lies and racism” would be considered by a court.

articles.title: UK and France believed to have vetoed UAE choice for UN secretary general
articles.summary: Costa Rican diplomat remains frontrunner but needs to win over two more permanent members of security council
body: The UK and France are believed to have effectively vetoed a controversial United Arab Emirates diplomat in a vote for the next UN secretary general, ostensibly over the UAE’s alleged links to atrocities in Sudan.
The search for a new chief diplomat for the world remained deadlocked on Friday after the UN security council’s ninth straw poll once again did not settle on a candidate.

The Costa Rican diplomat Rebeca Grynspan remains the frontrunner. In Friday’s poll she collected enough votes (10) to win the position, but the winner must also have no votes against from any of the security council’s “P5” permanent members – the US, UK, France, Russia and China – of which she collected two.

At more than 100 days, the vote to replace the current secretary general, António Guterres, is already the longest in UN history. His second term ends on 31 December. Another vote is scheduled for next week.
Should she overcome the two security council countries who oppose her – believed to be the US and Russia – then Grynspan would become the first woman to lead the UN.
Second on the latest ballot was Argentina’s Rafael Grossi, with eight “encourage” but three “discourage” votes from among the P5.

The Emirati diplomat Lana Nusseibeh, who had been a late entry into the race, received seven votes for but three against from the permanent members, a potentially insurmountable hurdle. Given her public support from the US and Russia and, according to multiple sources, it appeared likely she was effectively vetoed by the UK, France and China.

There has been widespread criticism over her candidacy due to the UAE’s ongoing links to the brutal conflict in Sudan. Nearly 70 MPs wrote to the UK foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, arguing Nusseibeh was not a “credible candidate” because she had “repeatedly denied and dismissed” reports by a UN panel of experts linking the UAE to atrocities in Sudan.
Related: Race to be next UN secretary general exposes divisions among world powers

Consistent reporting from the UN panel and rights groups says the UAE has hired mercenaries for, and provided weapons to, the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), the Sudanese paramilitary group the UN and US have determined has committed genocide in Darfur. The UAE denies involvement.

Nusseibeh has taken a leave of absence from her ministerial post in the UAE government, “mindful of the obligations of independence” the UN role would require, adding that “the horrific conflict in Sudan will be the litmus test of the success of an incoming secretary general”.

China’s opposition to Nusseibeh is grounded in its commitment to an unwritten convention that the secretary general’s position observes a geographic rotation, so all parts of the globe are ultimately represented: while the rotation principle has been ignored before, it is now the “turn” of Latin America or the Caribbean to hold the post.

The process of electing the world’s chief diplomat is an arcane one, controlled by the security council, and dominated by the council’s five permanent members who wield an effective veto. Candidates need nine “encourage” votes from the 15 nations on the council: five permanent members (P5) and 10 elected members (E10). But the P5 carry an effective veto as a winning candidate must have the support of all five permanent members.
Elected members vote with white ballots, permanent members vote with red ballots. Voting is never disclosed but tallies are distributed through unofficial channels.
Daniel Safran-Hon, a senior adviser at the International Peace Institute who formerly worked in the UN secretary general’s executive office, said Grynspan was the “undisputed frontrunner”.
He said the Costa Rican, who is the head of the UN conference on trade and development (UNCTAD), needed to win over the remaining two P5 members resisting her candidacy.

“It is all speculation at this stage, but I would speculate that it’s not impossible. It’s not easy because the fact is that she’s been trying for a while to peel off American opposition, but she is the undisputed frontrunner: other candidates face a steeper hill.”

Grynspan has invoked her Jewish heritage to argue for the importance of ending conflict; her agency, UNCTAD, has exhaustively documented the economic damage wrought by Israel’s long-term occupation of the Palestinian territories. If elected, she would be the UN’s first Jewish secretary general.

She told the UN general assembly: “Peace is what made it possible for my parents, two refugees from the second world war, to find respect and dignity in a small country, Costa Rica. I am the daughter of this peace, a demonstration of what peace makes possible.”

articles.title: Spain frees wealthy US-sought activist on bail as Irish police raid Dublin home
articles.summary: Pro-Palestinian donor James ‘Fergie’ Chambers released as court considers extradition request
body: In a blur of events surrounding the Trump administration’s effort to extradite James “Fergie” Chambers, Spain released the wealthy US activist and donor on bail even as Irish police raided a Dublin house owned by Chambers and his partner, Stella Schnabel, acting on a request from US authorities.

Chambers’s case is the first known instance of the US seeking to extradite a citizen over alleged support for Hamas, an accusation apparently tied to an international money-laundering charge in the criminal complaint underpinning the extradition request and donations to organizations helping Palestinians in Gaza.

Speaking outside Madrid’s Aranjuez prison upon his release on Friday, Chambers called the charges against him “baseless”, adding that his release was “hopefully the first step in recognizing that internationally”.
Related: US seized American heir’s cellphone in violation of treaty agreement, lawyer says

Chambers also said: “Spain is a country that has stood on the right side of this most important issue of our time, that has stood on the right side of the genocide, and where this is some reason and some justice.”

An appeals court ordered the conditional release on Friday due to issues surrounding the legally required US translation of the extradition request’s core documents into Spanish, first reported on by the Guardian. He had been detained since 10 July, when Spanish authorities arrested him in Ibiza.
The order asserts that the translation issues cause “a diminishment, at least for the time being, in the solidity or foundation of the extradition request”.

Chambers’s release follows a separate decision on Thursday by the three-judge panel at the high court tasked with deciding on the extradition to pause the proceedings in order to evaluate the impact of the alterations the US made to the original, machine-made translation of the extradition request into Spanish.

The Guardian detailed four examples of the alterations on 7 November and the US admitted to tampering with the translation, calling them “substantial [and] inadvertent” on 17 November – and citing the same four examples. Chambers’s defense team has asserted for weeks that there are as many as 30 such alterations.

The changes introduced prejudicial notions with specific legal implications that in turn wound up in the Spanish prosecutor’s report on the case, Aitor Martínez, a member of Chambers’s defense team, told the Guardian earlier this week. The judges must consider the prosecutor’s report in deciding on the extradition request.

The high court was expected to rule on the extradition this week, following a 13 November hearing. But as of Thursday’s decision, the deadline has been extended indefinitely as the judges evaluate the translation, including a 345-page report submitted by the defense team that identifies 30 “incriminating changes” Trump administration officials made to a translation prepared by DeepL, “an AI-first translation platform”, according to its website.
The decision also gives the prosecutor an opportunity to address the issue in writing, after dismissing it in the 13 November hearing by referring to “supposed translation errors”.

Chambers’s views and donations to progressive and humanitarian projects have been extensively profiled in US media, including his controversial public comments on Israel and Gaza. A week after the 7 October 2023 Hamas attacks on Israel, he posted on X about Israel’s response: “Stop calling it ‘collective punishment’/There’s nothing to be ‘punished’ for/No faction of the Palestinian resistance, Hamas or other, has done *anything* wrong/It’s simply genocide/Like it has been.”
The heir to $250m from his family’s business, Cox Enterprises, is being sought in extradition because of such views, his defense team has asserted throughout the case.

Meanwhile, the Irish Garda Síochána, acting on a request from US authorities, raided a Dublin house owned by Chambers and Schnabel on Wednesday, destroying the front door and removing electronic items and other possessions, according to their attorney in Ireland, Ciarán Mulholland.

Schnabel, who is five months pregnant, said: “It is difficult to see this raid as anything other than a desperate fishing expedition by the US authorities to find evidence to bolster their case against Fergie.”

The attorney told the Guardian that the raid was the result of a “mutual legal assistance” request from the US – and that such a request “wouldn’t give [the Garda Síochána] permission to kick in the doors of someone’s dwelling in Ireland”.

“It’s unusual for the Irish state to be acting in such a clandestine manner,” Mulholland said. He has asked authorities to produce a search warrant and an itemized list of what was taken. “My fear is that whatever was taken has been put on a plane and taken to the US,” he added.
“This [extradition case] shows the complete disregard for due process … that the Trump administration seems to have,” Mulholland said.

articles.title: Solange Alexandre obituary
articles.summary: French resistance fighter who founded and led a 30-strong group operating around Le Mans and Tours
body: Solange Alexandre, who has died aged 104, was one of the founders and leaders of a French resistance group that carried out a series of attacks on German troops around the cities of Le Mans and Tours, cutting supply and communications lines, and making hit-and-run attacks on convoys moving north into Normandy.

Then named Solange Dubuisson, she was 17 and training to be a teacher in Le Mans, in the north-west of the country, when the Germans overran France in 1940. Her father was wounded in the first world war in 1917, while her mother’s first husband had died fighting the Germans in the same war.

“The words homeland and honour were very important to us,” she said. “They were in my blood. I was immersed in that from a very young age.” The German occupation and the willingness of those like the Vichy France leader Marshal Philippe Pétain to collaborate “put hatred in my heart”.

So when Charles de Gaulle, who had gone to London to set up a government in exile, broadcast a call to the French people to never give up, she was inspired by his insistence that “the flame of French resistance must not and will not be extinguished”, and decided to fight. “From that moment, I knew I had to join up.”

She joined a local resistance group that was part of the OCM, the Organisation Civile et Militaire, working as a courier under the codename Corlay, often cycling vast distances delivering messages between groups as far west as Rennes in Brittany and north into Normandy. As a former gymnastics champion, she was extremely fit and up to the task.
While working with the group she met and fell in love with Guy Déliot, a former gendarme who had deserted after refusing to arrest a Jewish couple and joined the same resistance group.
Twice the Gestapo came for me. And twice I slipped through their hands

In April 1944, they decided to set up their own group, along with Dubuisson’s friend Michel Gadois and his brother, Jean, at Étang du Pas-de-Boeuf (Ox Passage Pond), a wooded area around a small lake north of Ruillé-sur-Loir in Sarthe.

The 30-strong “Pas-de-Boeuf” group was made up of a mix of men who had gone on the run to avoid deportation to Germany as forced labourers, survivors from a resistance group in the Vendée in western France which had been broken up by the Gestapo, and two allied airmen, an American and a Canadian, whose planes had been shot down.

Dubuisson took charge of the group, who lived in the forests and were supplied with food by local farmers while carrying out sabotage operations, destroying telephone lines, blocking roads and making small hit-and-run attacks against the Germans at night.

Under sustained fire from allied aircraft by day, and with no air cover from the Luftwaffe, the German troops moving north into Normandy were forced to hide under cover during the day and travel at night, making them vulnerable to small-scale ambushes. The impact of the group’s attacks meant the Germans were constantly trying to track them down. “Twice the Gestapo came for me,” Dubuisson later recalled. “And twice I slipped through their hands.”

On 8 August 1944, the day Le Mans was liberated, she and a dozen members of her group were returning from an attempt to sabotage a munitions train on the Tours-Le Mans railway line, when they heard that some German troops who had stolen horses were stationed at a farm just outside Ruillé-sur-Loir and, believing there was only a small number of them, decided to attack it, kill the Germans and retrieve the horses. But they were spotted by a sentry and found themselves under fire from around 80 German soldiers.
“We might have killed 20 or 30 of them,” she later said. But while they were retreating, Michel Gadois was wounded and captured. “He was finished off with a bullet to the head.”

She ended the war as a sub-lieutenant in the Forces Françaises de l’Intérieur, the Free French amalgamation of the various resistance groups, in charge of a department taking care of resistance members who had been deported or imprisoned by the Germans.
Born in Mamers, a small town in the Sarthe department of north-west France, she was the daughter of Marguerite and Albert Dubuisson, a gendarme.

A month before VE Day, she married Déliot. He rejoined the gendarmerie and was sent to work in the French overseas territories, initially in New Caledonia, where Solange took a job as secretary general of the chamber of agriculture. They had two daughters and a son.

When Déliot was killed during riots in Martinique in 1960, she returned to Le Mans and resumed teaching. She retired in 1978. A few years later, she married Bernard Alexandre, and after his death became an ardent campaigner for the right to die with dignity, serving as the Sarthe departmental delegate of ADMD (the Association pour le Droit de Mourir avec Dignité) for 16 years.

In 2022, on her 100th birthday, a ceremony was held in Ruillé-sur-Loir to rename the town square the Place Solange Dubuisson Alexandre. Expressing her thanks to those attending she said: “I am very proud, even if it is only a few weeks, or a few months, before I die.”
Alexandre twice turned down the Légion d’honneur, saying that she had merely done her patriotic duty, but was eventually persuaded to accept it in 2024.
Two of her children, Jean-Pierre and Françoise, predeceased her. She is survived by her daughter Marie-France.
• Solange Rose Marguerite Alexandre, French resistance fighter, born 9 September 1922; died 8 November 2026

articles.title: Russian missiles and drone hit Poland during attacks on Ukraine
articles.summary: Polish PM calls strikes, which took place amid western military exercises, ‘an intentional provocation’ by Moscow
body: Two Russian cruise missiles and a jet-powered drone crashed in Poland, according to officials, during Russian air attacks on Ukraine that took place amid major western military exercises by allied countries.
Poland accused Moscow of “provocation” after the strikes in the south-east area of the Nato country.
Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said it was “one of the largest attacks” since the full-scale Russian invasion in 2022, with at least eight people killed and nearly 30 injured in Ukraine.
“The Russians spread this attack across many cities and regions of Ukraine. Absolutely all the targets were ordinary civilian infrastructure – things that literally sustain people’s lives,” he said.

Zelenskyy said Russia’s president, Vladimir Putin, went ahead with the strike after “weak meetings” with the US president, Donald Trump, and China’s Xi Jinping, and his “failure to attempt to somehow redraw the world”.
The Ukrainian president added: “Russia is trying to compensate for its military and diplomatic impotence with precisely this kind of terror.”
Poland’s defence minister, Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, confirmed three violations of Polish airspace, with no injuries reported.

He said he believed it was “not accidental” that the incident took place on the same day as major western military exercises involving troops from 11 countries in the “coalition of the willing”, including the UK.
The incidents were reported in Nowy Lipowiec, Mołodycz and Rudnik nad Sanem in south-eastern Poland, between 30 miles (50km) and 60 miles from Nowa Dęba, where the exercises are taking place.
Poland’s prime minister called the incident “an intentional provocation” by Russia.

Donald Tusk said he had spoken with Nato’s secretary general, Mark Rutte – who will visit Warsaw on Saturday – who agreed with him that “it does not seem to be a coincidence” that the attack took place on the night before the drills.
“It clearly shows … that coming months … will certainly pose great challenges for all of us,” he said.

“Today’s incident shows clearer than ever before why Poland must participate in decisions on Ukraine’s future,” he added, arguing that Warsaw has a “better understanding” of the threat posed by Russia.

Rutte said on X: “Spoke with @donaldtusk about the grave violations of Polish airspace overnight. NATO jets were scrambled in response. We stand in solidarity with Poland and will continue to strengthen our ability to deter and defend.

“This incident is clearly dangerous - a consequence of Russia’s ongoing war against Ukraine. I condemn Russia’s attacks as well as its ongoing war. We continue to stand united as Allies and will continue to support Ukraine.”

​The UK defence secretary, Wes Streeting, who is in Poland for the exercises, described the incursion as “very serious” in a post on X, adding: “The impact of Russia’s illegal war is being felt across Ukraine and increasingly in neighbouring countries. The UK stands in solidarity with our allies.”
Maj Gen Ireneusz Nowak, commander of the operational command of the Polish armed forces, said as many as 11 objects had been identified as posing a danger to Polish airspace.

He also highlighted the unprecedented scale of the overnight attack on Ukraine, saying Russia used seven bombers and fired 26 Kalibr cruise missiles, 72 Kh-101 cruise missiles and more than 500 drones.

Air traffic control at Rzeszów-Jasionka airport – an international passenger hub and major transit point for military aid to Ukraine – was briefly evacuated overnight, for the first time since the start of the full-scale war in Ukraine.
After the incidents, Tusk summoned army and security service chiefs to an emergency meeting to discuss the situation.
Ukraine’s foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, said the latest violations “demonstrate the threats posed by Russian aggression to the whole of Europe and the transatlantic community”.

He added: “While Moscow tries to initiate discussions about the ‘new security architecture of Europe’, Russian missiles and drones directly undermine the existing security order in Europe. The first step toward strengthening it would probably be to cease such attacks.”
Polish authorities repeatedly warned in recent months against potential security incidents as they feared an escalation in Russia’s war against Ukraine.
In July, a Russian Kh-101 cruise missile fell in Poland’s Lublin region after veering off course during a nightly Russian attack on Ukraine.
In September last year, more than 20 Russian drones crossed into Polish airspace, with Tusk warning that the country was “closer to military conflict than at any time since the second world war”.
In November 2022, a Russian missile Kh-55 crashed near Bydgoszcz, more than 300 miles from Ukraine’s territory, but was only discovered in early 2023.

articles.title: Young people across Europe stage coordinated ‘fight for our future’ protests
articles.summary: Activists in more than 20 countries demonstrate over cost of living, learning conditions and rising military spending
body: Students and young workers have taken to the streets in more than 20 European countries in coordinated protests over the surging cost of living and housing, deteriorating learning conditions and rising military spending.

Activists from more than 50 groups in countries including Belgium, France, Germany, Greece, Italy, Portugal, Spain and the UK held rallies on Friday, lighting flares, burning cardboard models of tanks and waving placards, many reading “fight for our future”.

Calling it Europe’s biggest coordinated youth protest of recent years, the Youth Strike coalition said demonstrations were planned in about 400 cities under the slogan “fight for our future, not their wars”.

It made five broad demands, including an end to militarisation and conscription; structural investment in education and welfare; solidarity with Palestine; climate and social justice, and a “radical transformation of the system we live in”.

An Italian organiser, Alessandro di Miceli, said the Europe-wide protests were “to claim our right to a better and dignified future”. Specific demands differed from country to country, he said, but were all “deeply connected between each other”.

A Portuguese organiser, Leonor Chicó, said: “As young people, we know that we must organise and fight for our future, because no one else will do it for us.” Governments “show us every day that the needs of our generation are not their priority”, she said.

Shabbir Lakha from the UK-based Stop The War coalition said the mobilisation was “a crucial step towards building a lasting international movement capable of bringing together young people, students and workers around common demands”.

After weeks of demonstrations across several countries sparked by long-running French school protests, governments are struggling to respond to growing calls for affordable housing, functioning public services and greater social equality.

Among the organisers of Friday’s rallies in France were the gilets jaunes (yellow vests), whose protests rocked the country in 2018 and 2019, while in Germany, about 1,000 students demonstrated in Berlin over fears of a return to compulsory military service.

In Rome, Milan and other Italian cities, tens of thousands protested as the country’s largest trade union, the CGIL, ⁠staged a general strike against ⁠the economic policies of the prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, which it described as the country’s call for change.

“We ​are living under a government that is cutting healthcare and education, taking away our present and trying to rob us of our future,” said Laura Peritore, 24, a university student. “We will not back down and will take our future back.”

At a youth-led demonstration in London, marchers waved banners reading: “No to war, racism, climate crisis, capitalism.” In Spain, the protests fell on the anniversary of the death of the late dictator Francisco Franco.
Agence France-Presse and Reuters contributed reporting

articles.title: Gen Waheed Kakar obituary
articles.summary: Pakistani army chief who was noted for his admirable stance in not seeking civilian power during a leadership crisis in 1993
body: Waheed Kakar, the chief of army staff in the Pakistan army from 1993 until 1996, who has died aged 89, was notable for refusing to seek power outside his official role, in a country with a long history of military rulers.

In July 1993, confronted with a political crisis between the prime minister, Nawaz Sharif, and the president, Ghulam Ishaq Khan, instead of taking power himself and dissolving the civilian government as other military chiefs before him had done, Kakar secured the resignation of both civilian leaders and allowed elections to be held.
This chapter in Pakistani history is remembered as the “Kakar formula” – a rare occasion when a military chief distanced himself from civilian politics.

The general elections that were held as a result brought Benazir Bhutto to power. Just before Kakar’s term was due to finish in 1996, Bhutto sent repeated offers, direct and indirect, to him to continue as the army chief. But Kakar refused and said: “I am going home.” Bhutto described him as “a totally non-interfering army chief. He was an honourable man.”

His rise to power had in itself been unexpected, and came after the sudden death of Gen Asif Nawaz Janjua in January 1993. There was a deadlock for the selection of his successor as army chief, and both Sharif and Khan had their own favourites.
Unlike other military leaders, he chose to stay out of the spotlight

In seniority, Kakar was the fifth general in line for the powerful position. As the deadlock persisted, and since he was the only one to have no connections to either man, Kakar was nominated. According to Mariana Babar, a journalist with the English-language daily the News, who interviewed him soon afterwards, Kakar could hardly believe he was the new military chief.

It was Kakar’s first and last interview. Unlike other military leaders, he chose to stay out of the spotlight. “Remaining apolitical was part of his personality from the early days of his services. We don’t know who his favourite politician or political party was. Even after his retirement, he gave no clue,” Babar told me.

The son of Sardar Abdul Hameed Khan, a civil contractor, and Anwar Sultan, Kakar was born in British India, in the north-western city of Peshawar, which became part of Pakistan at partition. His uncle was the independence campaigner and politician Abdur Rab Nishtar. The family belonged to the Pashtun Kakar tribe and had moved to Peshawar from the south-western province of Balochistan.

Kakar studied at Edwardes College in the city, and joined the Pakistan military in 1956. Rising through the ranks, he saw combat and wars with India in 1965 and 1971, attended the Command and Staff College in Canada, and later studied at the National Defence College in Rawalpindi.

During his time as head of the army, Kakar forced the retirement of two powerful generals: Asad Durrani, who was accused of interfering in politics and distributing funds to an election alliance led by Sharif; and Gen Javed Nasir, former chief of Pakistan’s powerful ISI military intelligence agency, who was alleged to have supported fundamentalists and extremists.

In 1995, at least 38 military officers, including Maj Gen Zahirul Abbasi, planned to assassinate Kakar, Bhutto and other members of the senior military and civilian leadership, and to impose a military coup. They also plotted to proclaim a caliphate, with Abbasi as Amirul Momeneen – “leader of the faithful”. But the plan was thwarted, their arms were confiscated and they were arrested.

After his retirement in 1996, Kakar disappeared into the shadows. He did not take any political positions or head any government department, as would be the norm for former military officers. Former chiefs were occasionally invited to give their insights and suggestions at military headquarters, and Kakar would take part in those gatherings to share his opinions. According to Babar, his advice would always be: “Please keep religion out of the army.”
He is survived by his wife, Yasmin, whom he married in 1966, and their son and daughter.
• Abdul Waheed Kakar, army officer, born 23 March 1937; died 26 October 2026

articles.title: ‘As he veered towards us, fear set in’: outrage as driver not arrested after killing three at First Nations ceremony
articles.summary: After a driver crashed into people at a Tsawwassen ceremony, police suggested he’d had a ‘medical incident’
body: It was a cool, overcast morning in late September when members of the Tsawwassen First Nation gathered outside a shopping mall near Vancouver.
Two hand-carved house posts, carrying the history and identity of the community, were to be raised in a ceremony marking the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation.
Earl “Junior” Holland was among the people who arrived early to the Tsawwassen Mills mall, joining his wife and 12-year-old daughter, who had been asked to brush the posts with cedar and bless them.
“It was a very special day for her and the family,” said Holland. “This would be the first cultural work she was going to do for the community as a youth.”
She would also be under the watchful, proud gaze of her grandmother, elder Virginia Splockton, a fixture of Tsawwassen gatherings who often provided blessings and songs for major events.
“If you knew her, chances are she had cooked for you,” said Holland. “She was immensely proud of her community and family. She was someone just overflowing with love and kindness.”

Roughly 800ft away, Manpreet Singh, who knew nothing of the First Nations gathering, had arrived at the mall with his family, including his 11-month old daughter. He had just stepped out of his vehicle when a black pickup, towing an equipment trailer, backed into it, crunching it against another parked car.

Singh thought it was an accident and tried to wave down the truck, he told the local Sher-e-Punjab Radio station. But the driver, who briefly made eye contact with him, backed the trailer once more into Singh’s vehicle before driving off. Terrified, Singh called his cousin and then 911.

Less than 15 minutes later, the preparations for the First Nations pole-raising were shattered as a black truck towing an equipment trailer breached the curb, hit the unsuspecting group and eventually smashed into a wall.

Splockton was killed. So was wilapiya (also known as Barb Joe), a key knowledge keeper of the Tsawwassen First Nation. Two other people were rushed to hospital by helicopter, where one would die from her injuries.
Later that day, police issued a news release saying that “preliminary information” from the scene suggested the driver had experienced a medical emergency.
The incident was “not related” to the Truth and Reconciliation Walk, they said, adding: “There is no ongoing risk to public safety.”
The driver was brought to the hospital and released later that day. No charges have been filed.
In the weeks since, what was meant to be a celebration of identity and resilience has instead become a maddening search for answers.

Delta police did not return multiple phone messages or to a contact by email to discuss the incident, the investigation, or a timeline of the police response. Mike Whiteley, staff sergeant of the department’s media relations team, said in a statement that police “are not in a position to provide additional details beyond what has already been released publicly”.
Holland said the moments leading up to the crash have weighed heavily on his family.
He recalled his excitement and pride at his daughter’s participation in the event. But then he saw the pickup truck approaching.
“As he veered towards us, fear set in. I worried something bad might happen.”
He rushed his wife and daughter inside the mall to safety.
Then he returned outside to see crumpled bodies. An ambulance dispatcher directed him how to triage the wounded, including Splockton.

“It was really traumatizing because I saw my mother-in-law lying on the ground. At that moment she was breathing. She was alive. I wanted to stay with her. But they told me I needed to go to the next person and check on them. It was so hard to leave her,” he said. “But we needed to see who we could save.”

Neither the crowd nor emergency crew could save wilapiya, a matriarch who had spent years working to protect and pass on Tsawwassen First Nation language and traditions. Community members drummed and sang as the bodies of the two women were moved into a coroner’s vehicle.

A third woman, Gwenyth Brigid Dwyn, died days later in the hospital. Kevin Li, hired by the First Nation to record video footage, spent nearly a week in the intensive care unit after suffering extensive injuries.
But even as emergency crews tended to the injured, police were beginning to shape the public account of what had happened.

According to Mandalena Lewis, an independent journalist who runs She(Bites) Media and first reported many of the events, Delta police first notified the public on social media roughly an hour after the incident, describing it as a “collision” that “appear[ed]” to involve a medical emergency.
In a press release, they said the incident was “not related” to the Truth and Reconciliation Walk.
What they did not mention was Singh’s vehicle also being hit by what he said was a black truck towing an equipment trailer minutes earlier.
While police did not say whether they knew about the earlier collision when they issued their first public statement, Singh said it came roughly 30 minutes after he spoke to them about it.

Holland said his experience that morning clashes with the details later released by police. “It feels they had not even started an investigation before they basically concluded there was no investigation,” said Holland.

For some in the Tsawwassen community, the police statements evoked another incident in British Columbia in 2022, when a man named Richard Albert Manuel drove his pickup truck into a crowd marching for residential school survivors.

The Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP) initially said the incident did not appear to be targeted, and that Manuel striking marchers with his car did not have “anything specifically to do with the people marching or their cause”.
Instead, after interviewing the driver two days later, the RCMP said Manuel had been “impatient” and trying to get around the group “despite the safety risk”.

After community members compiled evidence and brought it to the police, including what the judge concluded were “racist slurs and derogatory remarks” he made, he was charged and later convicted in September 2024 of “dangerous operation of a motor vehicle” and served a nine-month sentence in the community.
Holland said he finds that incident impossible to ignore when considering the police response to the tragedy at the mall.
“It just feels like it’s repeated over and over again. Our people are constantly having to fight for ourselves,”he said.

Fifteen days after the incident, on 14 October, police issued another statement, saying the “medical event” possibility was still under investigation, but that “if the evidence establishes criminality”, then charges would be laid. They said investigators were “examining the movements of the involved vehicle on the Tsawwassen Mills property before the pedestrians were struck, including an earlier collision” and that they had “not reached any final conclusions regarding the cause of the collisions”.
“Investigators are working through a significant amount of information, and it is important that we not reach conclusions before that work is complete,” Whiteley added in the statement.

Holland said some of the affected families went to the police the following day out of frustration and disbelief, including at the declaration that the department “continues to communicate with the affected families”. “They put out a statement that they’re talking to the families. But they had not reached out to us at all. We’ve had questions and it’s just been silence from them. We were angry they told the public they’ve been talking to us when they haven’t.”
The lack of information has prompted Tsawwassen First Nation members to assemble their own evidence, gathering eyewitness accounts and video footage.

“These families are just completely torn up, and yet they’re basically having to do all this work themselves to try and get answers,” said Lewis. As part of her investigation of the events, Lewis tracked down Singh after hearing him on local radio and was shocked to learn police had not publicly disclosed that a black truck towing an equipment trailer had already struck another vehicle nearby, twice, minutes beforehand. “I’m just dumbfounded by the way this is being handled and conveyed to the public,” she said.

In an audio recording reviewed by the Guardian, Delta’s chief constable, Harjinder Singh Sidh, said in a community meeting that the police were concerned about spreading fear. Following the deaths of 11 people in April 2025, when an SUV rammed through a street festival in Vancouver, he said officers wanted to reassure the Tsawwassen First Nation that the latest incident was not intentional and to “calm the community down”.

But members of the First Nation say that, in apparently trying to prevent panic, police instead communicated a degree of certainty about the motives of the driver. “They could have just said: ‘We are investigating.’ Why did they have to rush to say it was a medical emergency, when so many people on the ground experienced something so different?” said Holland.
The post-raising ceremony, he noted, was meant to be a moment to recognize the resilience of his people.
“This was supposed to be a day for celebration,” he said. “Now we’re terrified to attend larger events. We’re scared to stand proudly in public.”

articles.title: UK and EU close to post-Brexit deal as they agree 100,000 youth mobility cap
articles.summary: Two sides find provisional compromise on scheme but food and farming negotiations go down to the wire
body: British and European negotiators were closing in on a reset deal on Thursday night as they provisionally agreed to allow 100,000 EU citizens to come to the UK every year under a new mobility scheme.
It is understood the EU dropped its demands at the last minute that its students should pay home tuition fees if they attended British universities in a concession to get the deal over the line.

The UK had strongly resisted EU text on the table committing it to home fees instead of “significantly reduced” international fees, but a compromise was hammered out before 10pm, with a “supplementary agreement” to work out the details within the next six months.
Brussels insiders said the EU had kicked the can down the road and agreed not to mention the tuition fees rate in the declaration, with further negotiations to follow in the next six months.
As talks went into the night, EU sources suggested both sides were on track for an agreement within the next day.

On Friday morning, the UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, said the UK and Europe were “stronger together”, adding: “The test for this summit is simple: does it make life better for people in Britain? That is what I will deliver in Brussels today – cutting costs, keeping prices down in the supermarkets and creating opportunities for young people.”

The Reform UK leader, Nigel Farage, told the BBC that Burnham’s approach amounted to a “betrayal”. He said: “He’s trying to do it incrementally but it’s perfectly clear that this very very soon becomes a debate about do we rejoin or do we stay out.”
But he acknowledged that for food exporters a deal on agricultural standards would make things “a little bit easier”.

On the eve of a summit in Brussels, the EU was “going into a landing zone” on the question of a British voice in shaping the rules under a food and drink agreement the government hopes to unveil on Friday, an EU source said.
There also seemed to be a compromise by France after a dispute among member states over how far Britain could be involved in shaping policies related to the food and drink deal.

The UK had demanded a “voting” role on some law-making in relation to food standards that France heavily opposed, and London eventually conceded on a point many think was unrealistic from the start. Instead, the UK will be consulted on new food laws, but the details on the level of involvement remain to be seen.

Earlier on Thursday the UK made concessions to increase the quota of EU citizens who could take part in a new youth mobility scheme, agreeing a cap of 100,000, instead of 50,000-80,0000 as previously sought.

It was also agreed to raise the age cap from 30 to 31.The number of young British people allowed to go to the EU under the scheme will be matched but could be higher, with some countries, including Germany, being prepared to take unlimited numbers each year.
With less than 24 hours to go before Burnham was due in Brussels for the summit with EU leaders, the two sides still needed to resolve some sticking points.
Speaking in general terms about the disagreements, another EU diplomat said: “It will go down to the wire. Our feeling is that the Brits have to move if they want a deal.”

A spokesperson for the British prime minister also described the talks as close, saying if an agreement was reached, the government would bring forward legislation, the cutting costs bill, to parliament next week.
Related: The Guardian view on Europe and Burnham: a future that can only be viewed through a glass darkly | Editorial

At the long-awaited summit, the EU and UK hope to sign three agreements, which are expected to add 0.4% to British GDP, including the highly prized food and drink deal that was a Labour manifesto commitment.
The deal, expected to come into force on 1 March 2028, requires the UK to align with EU rules on sanitary and phytosanitary (SPS) standards, making Britain a rule taker.

Asked about Britain’s status as a rule taker, No 10 said the Labour manifesto had aimed to build closer ties with the EU, adding: “We were obviously elected on a manifesto that promised to reset the relationship and seek to deepen ties with our European friends.”

According to EU sources, the UK has been pushing to have a formal role in EU committees involved in implementing existing and setting new SPS rules. An EU diplomat said: “They want to be able to shape decisions, not only implementation, but future decisions. That has always been a red line.”
Under the SPS proposal, the UK will agree to dynamically align with EU laws and will have a “voice” but “not be in the room” when laws are drafted.
A second diplomat from a country sympathetic to the British position said the European Commission had proposed an “extremely restrictive consultation mechanism” for the UK.

In contrast, the EU diplomat thought it was reasonable for a British representative to take part in the implementation of SPS legislation affecting the UK. “Of course the UK cannot vote in the council as a non-member state, but we feel that we need to be pragmatic about coordination and implementation,” they said.
Related: Andy Burnham is in danger of over-selling his big Brussels summit. What happens if he under-delivers? | Joël Reland

The issue proved difficult to resolve because it divided member states. France was perceived by other member states to be the main barrier to greater UK involvement in EU working groups on food and drink laws. “They are super principled on that point,” said a second EU diplomat.
The French government does not agree that it has been the main block, arguing that only a few member states wanted to accommodate the UK.

The issue raises the tensions at the heart of the UK’s status as a rule taker, and would be many times magnified were Britain to choose to enter the single market as a non-EU member state. The precise details of how the UK would be consulted on future food and farming rules remain unclear.

Burnham’s spokesperson suggested there was a UK-EU consensus that there would be no further incremental reset summits beyond the one on Friday until a full negotiation commenced on a longer-term, more stable relationship, such as rejoining the single market.
“After the summit, we will begin those discussions with our European partners about the realistic options for our longer-term relationship,” he said.

articles.title: Friday briefing: ​What are the implications of the ICJ’s landmark genocide ruling?
articles.summary: In today’s newsletter: ​For the first time the ICJ has ruled a state is responsible for genocide meaning the Rohingya can seek justice from Myanmar, setting a powerful precedent
body: Good morning. It’s a judgment of historic significance – one of the most consequential ever delivered by the International Court of Justice. Yesterday, it ruled Myanmar was guilty of committing genocide against the country’s Rohingya minority. It’s the first time a state, rather than individuals, has been found culpable of this most grave crime against humanity.

For survivors, bereaved families, and more than one million exiled Rohingya refugees, this offers the first semblance of justice. The result is final: the findings, punishments and restitutions determined cannot be appealed against. And the ramifications for others who face persecution around the world could be vast, as the exact wording of the verdict is carefully dissected.
In today’s First Edition, we unpack this landmark case, and ask what precedents it could set. That’s after this morning’s headlines.
UK news | A woman who was raped by strangers after being drugged by her husband has warned of “serious questions about how the law deals with consent”, as four men who abused her were convicted.

World news | China, Russia and the US say they have agreed a peace statement after an unprecedented trilateral summit, but the declaration made no mention of the wars in Ukraine and Iran caused by two of the participants.
Europe news | The UK-EU reset talks will go “down to the wire” as the British government battles to have a say in shaping future European food and farming rules.

Climate crisis | Every mention of fossil fuels has been expunged from the draft outcome of global climate talks, which were approaching their final hours on Thursday night, threatening to turn the UN summit into what campaigners called a “ghost Cop”.
AI | Anthropic closed its first day of trading on the US stock market about 17% higher than its initial public offering price.

The International Court of Justice (ICJ) in The Hague was packed yesterday morning, as its president delivered its milestone verdict. It took seven years for the case, raised by the Gambia, to reach this closing stage, and almost three hours for Judge Yuji Iwasawa to read through the final judgment.

In 2017, Myanmar’s military engaged in “indiscriminate killing”, “widespread sexual violence” and “executions”, the ruling declared. Villages were destroyed. Measures were introduced to limit the number of children Rohingya could have. Those fleeing were attacked. A “hate speech campaign” painted the Rohingya as “subhuman”.

Eventually, Yuji Iwasawa reached the pivotal line: “All evidence supports reasonable inference Myanmar’s security forces acted with genocidal intent”, adding a majority of nine judges on the 15-seat court agreed Myanmar “committed genocide against the Rohingya”.

Persecution of the Muslim Rohingya minority in majority Buddhist Myanmar can be traced back decades. In 1978, they were expelled from the country en masse. The government stripped Rohingya of their citizenship in the early 1980s – mass arrests and widespread violence followed. This volatile situation reached an apex in 2017: after Rohingya rebels attacked military posts, Myanmar’s response was genocidal. Yesterday, the court found more than 10,000 Rohingya were killed, including between 730 and 2000 children under five. Hundreds of thousands fled across the border to Bangladesh. Today, 1.2 million Rohingya remain displaced, many in Cox’s Bazar, the world’s largest refugee camp.

Guardian reporter Kaamil Ahmed was in the courtroom yesterday. His book, I Feel No Peace, documented the experiences of Rohingyas living in exile. Kaamil was in Cox’s Bazar in 2019, when the case was announced, where few believed this result would ever be realised.
“For many years, there’s been hope among community leaders,” Kaamil told me. “But still, they were prepared for disappointment.”

Once the verdict was returned, celebrations erupted around the building. Tinsel-like scarves were hung around the necks of the Gambia’s legal team. Outside, a Rohingya campaigner on a megaphone declared solidarity with other persecuted peoples.

The Rohingya can now think about the future. The ruling stipulated Myanmar must provide reparations and restitution: the safe return of Rohingya to their homes, the return or replacement of their property, and physical and mental rehabilitation.

“I’ve spoken to people living in refugee camps who are at last feeling hopeful,” Kaamil said. “Finally, they’re able to think about what’s next and how they might go home to Myanmar and rebuild their lives there.”

The ICJ was established in 1945, in the wake of the second world war, in efforts to re-establish a peacetime international order. It’s the United Nations’ highest court for legal disputes between states, though its caseload in recent years has increasingly focused on allegations of human rights violations.

In 1948, as the world grappled with the aftermath of the Holocaust, the Genocide Convention was passed by the UN general assembly. It formally made genocide a crime under international law. It is defined as the committing of any of five acts – killing, causing serious bodily or mental harm, imposing living conditions intended to, preventing births, or forcibly transferring children – if committed with “intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnic, racial or religious group”. The ICJ found Myanmar guilty of four of these charges.

Until now, only individuals had been successfully convicted of genocide in international courts: Rwandans including former prime minister Jean Kambanda; senior military figures in the former Yugoslavia and Cambodia. But no state had been found guilty of genocide until yesterday.

Nehal Bhuta is a Professor of International Law at the University of Edinburgh, and a member of Matrix Chambers. The ICJ’s conclusion that an entity, rather than a person, has committed genocide, Bhuta tells me, will have major repercussions. The bar to prove genocidal intent is high. “The court has found it’s not necessary to have evidence of individual intent by any particular leader or general or commander,” he says. “It changes our expectation of the conditions under which a court might reach a genocide conclusion.”

This case was also the first time the ICJ has made a final ruling on a genocide case brought by a third country. During its early stages, questions were raised as to whether the Gambia even had the right to take this case to court, given it is thousands of miles from Myanmar, and wasn’t directly affected. The ICJ found the Gambia was, in fact, eligible. “It’s the principle of erga omnes standing,” Bhuta says. Upholding the Genocide Convention is so important, that “any party to it has an interest in holding other states accountable.”

Across the world, lawyers are today combing through the dense 186 page judgment. Officially, the ICJ’s judgments each stand alone – they don’t formally set binding legal precedents for future cases. Still, its judges factor in previous decisions. “It’s actually very rare that they radically diverge from a legal conclusion that they’ve reached from case-to-case,” Bhuta says.

Four genocide-related cases remain pending at the ICJ, two related to Israel’s war on Gaza. South Africa has agued Israel is “engaging in and risks further engaging in genocidal acts against the Palestinian people in Gaza”. Separately, Nicaragua has lodged a case against Germany, accusing it of violating the Genocide Convention through its “political, financial and military support” of Israel, and for “defunding Unrwa.”

Certain conclusions will already have garnered the attention of the respective legal teams. One of the most dramatic conclusions reached by the court was in how a decision on genocidal intent was reached. Myanmar had argued it wasn’t committing genocide, but an operation of counter-insurgency, or even ethnic cleansing.
